strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 datasets with 6 different generative models, demonstrating consistent improvements (79-92% win rates) with rigorous reporting of mean and standard deviation over 10 runs

Clear theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) that establishes sufficient conditions for when modifying the terminal distribution reduces KLD, with explicit loss function (Eq. 4) designed to satisfy these conditions
Practical applicability: the framework seamlessly integrates with diverse existing models (both diffusion and flow-based) and is readily extensible
Well-motivated method design with principled connection between theory and practice through the JMCE algorithm
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple complementary metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID, ProbMSE, ProbMAE) providing multi-faceted assessment of improvements
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea of using better priors (mean and covariance) for diffusion models is well-established in prior work (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff); this work primarily combines these with explicit theory

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 justifies using true conditional covariance, but the method estimates sliding-window covariance instead, a simplification that may not satisfy theoretical conditions; minimal guidance provided for window size selection
Lack of rigorous statistical testing despite overlapping confidence intervals in many cases (e.g., Table 2: NsDiff); no significance tests to validate improvements, especially for modest differences

Missing key baseline comparisons: CARD (the seminal prior work on incorporating priors into diffusion models) and TsFlow are not included in experiments despite being relevant; unfair comparison with prior-informed baselines that use different prior incorporation mechanisms

Incomplete transparency on hyperparameter tuning: unclear whether λmin, wEigen, and window size were tuned uniformly across all methods or separately per dataset, which could bias results in favor of CW-Gen
Computational complexity not addressed: O(d³Tf) eigen-decomposition cost in CW-Diff is not analyzed; no runtime comparisons provided; no practical guidance on CW-Diff vs CW-Flow trade-offs
Limited dataset scope: maximum dimensionality is 137 (all datasets relatively small); no evaluation on truly high-dimensional time series where computational complexity would be problematic
Insufficient analysis of failure cases and method limitations: Solar Energy shows only 79.17% win rate but reasons are not analyzed; no discussion of when/why the method fails

Theorem 1 provides only sufficient conditions without tightness analysis: unclear how restrictive the condition (Eq. 3) is or when it holds in practice; Theorem 2 comparing to TMDM/NsDiff is relegated to appendix

Core ablation studies and sensitivity analyses (mean only vs. covariance only vs. both; sensitivity to window size and hyperparameters) mentioned as being in Appendix D but not discussed in main paper

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying specific limitations in prior work (TMDM, NsDiff) with well-articulated research questions
General framework integrating with 6 diverse baseline models, demonstrating broad applicability
Theorem 1 provides concrete sufficient conditions for KL divergence reduction with formal guarantees
Comprehensive experimental setup with 5 datasets, 6 metrics, and reported standard deviations; high win rates (79-92%)
Principled JMCE design using Cholesky decomposition and eigenvalue constraints with multi-term loss
weaknesses: Theory is limited and loose: Theorem 1 is intuitive but lacks finite-sample analysis, convergence rates, or guidance on required estimation accuracy; no proof of how tight condition (3) is

Significant theory-practice gap: JMCE uses sliding-window covariance while theory concerns true conditional covariance; loss function design in Eq. (4) appears post-hoc rather than derived from Theorem 1; hyperparameter choices lack justification

Empirical improvements on strong baselines are marginal and inconsistent: NsDiff actually degrades on ETTh1 CRPS (0.407→0.416); many gains within 1-2 standard deviations; no formal statistical significance testing
Claims are overstated: 'Consistent improvements' contradicted by metric-specific failures; 'distribution shift mitigation' lacks quantitative validation despite multiple mentions

Design choices insufficiently justified: Why specific loss term combination (L₂, L_SVD, Frobenius, eigenvalue penalty)? Ablation studies relegated to appendices. Hyperparameter settings (λ_min, window sizes) appear ad-hoc
Limited experimental scope: Only 5 standard benchmarks and recent generative models; no classical baselines (ARIMA, VAR) or simpler prior methods for comparison
Computational complexity analysis missing: O(d³T_f) mentioned but no runtime comparisons provided; practical cost-benefit unclear
Reproducibility concerns: Implementation details in appendices; code unavailable; hyperparameter rationale unexplained; key ablations (removing loss terms, hyperparameter sensitivity) not accessible

strengths: Principled theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 provides rigorous sufficient conditions for when conditional distribution replacement improves KL divergence, grounding the approach in theory
Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in prior work (CARD, TimeDiff, TMDM, NsDiff)
Sophisticated JMCE design using Cholesky decomposition, eigenvalue regularization, and loss function directly motivated by theory
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 datasets, 6 generative models, 6 metrics, with 10 runs and standard deviations
Consistent improvements demonstrated with high win rates (79-92%), particularly strong for correlation (ProbCorr) and sample quality (Conditional FID) metrics
General framework seamlessly integrating with diverse diffusion and flow-matching models; shows prior methods as special cases
Clear interpretability of conditional whitening operation: removes trends/seasonality and addresses heteroscedasticity/correlations
Strong improvements in point forecasting metrics (ProbMSE, ProbMAE) alongside probabilistic metrics
weaknesses: Marginal improvements over strongest baseline (NsDiff): e.g., ETTh1 CRPS actually increases (0.407→0.416); improvements often <5% with no statistical significance testing despite having standard deviations
Theorem 1's sufficient condition (Eq. 3) is complex with multiple norm terms; tightness unclear and practical verifiability not demonstrated; no empirical validation of condition satisfaction
Missing Theorem 2 comparison with TMDM/NsDiff relegated to appendix, preventing main-paper assessment of claimed theoretical advantages
No error propagation analysis: how do estimation errors in μ̂ and Σ̂ affect theoretical guarantees? Condition depends on unknown ground truth quantities
Sliding-window covariance assumption under-justified theoretically; why not condition on recent history? No ablation on window size selection despite varying across datasets (95 vs. 15)
Limited experimental scale: only 5 datasets, maximum dimensionality 137; no large-scale or truly high-dimensional experiments; no controlled distribution shift evaluation despite claims
Hyperparameter sensitivity under-explored: λ_min, w_Eigen choices lack justification; claim w_Eigen ∼ O(λ_min^{-1}) unsubstantiated; no sensitivity analysis provided
Computational complexity O(d³T_f) for CW-Diff not addressed; no wall-clock time comparisons provided; scalability to high-dimensional data unclear
Critical reproducibility gaps: implementation details in appendices, no code availability mentioned, limited guidance on hyperparameter selection for new datasets
Theoretical-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes 'good' estimators exist without formalizing bounds; no analysis of poor performance during early training; unclear how to verify condition (3) in practice

strengths: Rigorous theoretical foundation with Theorem 1 providing mathematically grounded sufficient conditions for when prior-informed terminal distributions improve generation quality
Well-motivated JMCE design directly addressing theoretical requirements from Theorem 1 with principled eigenvalue regularization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation integrating CW-Gen with 6 diverse generative models across 5 datasets with multiple metrics and consistent ~80-90% win rates
Extensive ablation studies (hyperparameter sensitivity, component analysis, architecture comparison) demonstrating thorough understanding and validation
Strong reproducibility with detailed algorithms, implementation details, computational optimization strategies, and code availability mentioned
Clear presentation with good visualizations and logical flow connecting theory to practice
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core technique: incorporating priors into diffusion models is established (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff), and conditional whitening is a standard change of variables

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes true conditional covariance but JMCE uses sliding-window approximation without theoretical justification; condition (3) is complex and unclear when it holds in practice
Inconsistent experimental results: CW-NsDiff sometimes underperforms baseline (e.g., Table 2: 0.431 vs 0.407 CRPS on ETTh1), and Solar Energy shows mixed results with some metrics worsening

Significant computational scalability concerns: O(d³) eigen-decomposition creates ~35x slowdown on Solar Energy (24,185s vs 684s); impractical for high-dimensional time series despite mentioned acceleration strategies
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: limited investigation of when Theorem 1's condition fails; unclear guidance on when to choose CW-Gen over NsDiff; appendix discussion of failures is post-hoc

Methodological concerns: JMCE trained separately and frozen (not jointly optimized with generative model), hyperparameter λmin=0.1 appears arbitrary with limited guidance for new datasets, potential validation leakage

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation establishing sufficient conditions (Theorem 1) for KL divergence reduction
Comprehensive experimental coverage integrating 6 generative models across 5 datasets with extensive ablation studies
Consistent empirical improvements shown across most model-dataset combinations (79-92% win rates)
Principled JMCE design with loss function directly motivated by theoretical bounds
Compelling visual evidence (Figure 2) demonstrating better capture of sample statistics and temporal patterns
Discussion of practical computational optimizations for efficiency improvements
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core idea of priors in diffusion models is established (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff); full covariance + whitening is incremental; whitening is standard statistical technique

Weak theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 provides only sufficient conditions without tightness analysis, convergence rates, or sample complexity; no empirical verification that condition (3) holds on datasets

Restrictive theory-practice gap: Condition (3) requires large signal ||μ||²₂ relative to estimation errors; paper acknowledges failure regimes (Appendix D) but provides no guidance on preventing degradation

Experimental rigor issues: no statistical significance testing; some improvements within noise (e.g., ETTh2 NsDiff: 0.370→0.369); degradations unexplained (SSSD Solar Energy: 0.350→0.555); limited dataset diversity
Critical scalability limitation: O(d³) complexity makes method impractical for high-dimensional data (Solar Energy: 8,120s vs 684s for baseline, 12× slowdown; training takes 24,185s)

JMCE design largely ad-hoc: sliding-window vs. conditional covariance choice unjustified; loss function combination (L₂, L_F, L_SVD) not principled; hyperparameters (λ_min=0.1, w_Eigen=50) tuned empirically without guidance

Inconsistent empirical results: some baselines degrade under CW (contradicting claims of universal improvement); win rate metric (91.67%) misleading as many improvements are <5%; no statistical significance bounds
Incomplete justification: no empirical stationarity validation despite 'rendering data stationary' claim; distribution shift mitigation shown only qualitatively; nuclear norm choice unexplained
Presentation and reproducibility: 36-page dense paper with key content in appendix; overstatements ('establish for the first time'); code URL blank; many hyperparameters with unclear setting strategy
Missing ablations and comparisons: no comparison with alternative covariance estimators; limited contrast with other prior-informed methods; DSPD/TsFlow comparison brief and univariate-only

strengths: Solid theoretical foundation with Theorem 1 providing sufficient conditions that directly motivate the loss function design and JMCE approach
Well-designed Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator that jointly learns conditional mean and covariance while explicitly controlling eigenvalues for numerical stability
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 datasets, 6 generative models, and multiple metrics (79-92% win rates), with consistent improvements (e.g., Conditional FID: 81.6→7.7 on ETTh1)
Extensive ablation studies examining hyperparameters, backbones, prior components, and training variants, providing strong evidence of design choices
Practical contributions including computational optimization via triangular inversion and end-to-end training variant
General framework seamlessly integrating with diverse diffusion and flow matching models
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem, intuitive figures, and logical progression from theory to method to experiments
weaknesses: Limited theoretical scope: Theorem 1 provides only sufficient conditions (not necessary), no tightness analysis, and KL divergence improvement is only one component of total error

Theory-practice gap with sliding-window covariance: Theorem 1 assumes true conditional covariance but JMCE estimates a different sliding-window proxy; approximation error and impact not rigorously analyzed
Incremental novelty over NsDiff: Core idea of incorporating priors is established; main novelty is joint estimation with eigenvalue control, which while useful is somewhat incremental

Significant computational limitations: O(d³) eigendecomposition makes high-dimensional data prohibitive (24k seconds for d=137 vs 156s for d=7); Solar Energy shows weakest improvements (79.17% win rate)
Mixed results on some metrics: QICE improvements inconsistent (0-83% win rate), suggesting method may not universally improve quantile calibration; high-dimensional datasets show weaker benefits
Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: λ_min=0.1 and w_Eigen=50 appear hand-tuned; Tables 12-13 show sensitivity but ablations don't justify choices for new datasets
End-to-end training (CW-E2E) shows worse QICE than pipeline variant (Table 18), raising stability concerns and suggesting the variant needs further investigation

Limited analysis of failure modes: While Appendix D discusses when condition (3) theoretically fails, no empirical characterization of which datasets/domains benefit most or when method should not be used
